name: The Hours We Invented: A History of Keeping Time
description: Shadows, dripping water, swinging weights and vibrating atoms: how people learned to count the days, divide them and agree on the time, from Stonehenge to atomic clocks.

checkpoints.name: Sun, moon and water
checkpoints.note: Stonehenge and the Egyptian and Maya calendars followed the sky, sundials and water clocks split the day, and Rome's calendar was tidied by Caesar into the Julian year.

checkpoints.name: Sacred and mechanical
checkpoints.note: Calendars of faith, such as the Hebrew and the Islamic, were fixed, the Anno Domini count of years from Christ's birth was proposed in 525, and the verge escapement made the first mechanical clocks possible.

checkpoints.name: Pendulum and reform
checkpoints.note: Hourglasses and clocks spread through towns. Galileo studied the pendulum, Huygens built the first accurate pendulum clock, and a papal reform created the Gregorian calendar.

checkpoints.name: Longitude and order
checkpoints.note: Harrison's marine chronometer solved the problem of finding longitude at sea. Wristwatches appeared, revolutionary France tried a calendar of ten-day weeks, and the railways forced towns to give up local time for standard time.

checkpoints.name: Quartz and atoms
checkpoints.note: Quartz clocks, then atomic clocks, set a steadier beat than the turning Earth itself, and since 1960 Coordinated Universal Time has kept the whole planet's clocks in step.
